samples.text:
The diagram shows how the food waste from a household is changed into compost. There are seven stages and it is a cycle.

At first, vegetable peelings and food scraps are collected in a kitchen caddy. Then the waste is put in a compost bin in the garden, and leaves and cardboard is added too. After that, the waste is broken down by worms and bacterias, this is decomposition.

Next, the compost is mixed every 2–3 weeks for adding air. This is called turning. Then the compost is left for 6–12 months until it becomes dark and crumbly, so this stage takes the longest time.

When the compost is ready, it is spread on the soil in the garden. Finally, vegetables are grown in the soil and people eat them. The scraps from these vegetables go back to the kitchen caddy, and the cycle start again.

Overall, the process starts and finishes in the kitchen, and the food waste is not wasted because it helps to grow new vegetables which people can eat again.
samples.why: Basic overview at the end · all stages and timings covered in order · mechanical linking · repetitive vocabulary · agreement, word form and comma splice errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The diagram illustrates the process by which food waste from the home is turned into compost and then used to grow food.

Overall, the process is cyclical and consists of seven stages. It begins and ends in the kitchen, since the scraps from the vegetables that are grown return to the caddy, and the longest stage is maturing, which can take up to a year.

Firstly, vegetable peelings and other food scraps are collected in a kitchen caddy. This waste is then placed in a compost bin in the garden along with leaves and cardboard. Inside the bin, worms and bacteria break the waste down, a stage known as decomposition, and the mixture is turned every two to three weeks so that air is added to it.

After that, the compost is left to mature for between 6 and 12 months until it become dark and crumbly. It is then spread on the soil, where vegetables are grown. Once these vegetables have been harvested and eaten, the scraps are returned to the kitchen caddy, and the whole cycle begins again.
samples.why: Clear overview stating the cycle and longest stage · logical progression with a range of cohesive devices · some less common vocabulary (crumbly, mature) · mostly error-free with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The diagram depicts the seven-stage cycle through which household food waste is converted into compost and ultimately helps to produce new food.

The most notable feature of the process is its circular nature: it starts with scraps collected in the kitchen and ends with vegetables whose leftovers return to that same point. Of the individual stages, maturing is by far the most protracted, lasting between six months and a year, far longer than the two- to three-week interval between turnings.

To begin with, peelings and food scraps are gathered in a kitchen caddy before being transferred to a garden compost bin, where they are combined with leaves and cardboard. Worms and bacteria then set about decomposing this material, and the contents of the bin are turned every two to three weeks to aerate them.

Next, the compost is left to mature for 6–12 months, by which time it has become dark and crumbly. It is then spread on the soil and used to grow vegetables, which are eventually eaten. The scraps from these return to the caddy, allowing the cycle to repeat indefinitely.
samples.why: Perceptive overview emphasising the circular nature and longest stage · stages linked seamlessly · precise vocabulary (protracted, aerate, decomposing) · wide range of structures · error-free.
